title: Sanctions against Ernst & Young LLP and Mr Christopher Voogd
text:
IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL OF THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
(1) ERNST & YOUNG LLP

(2) MR CHRISTOPHER JULES VOOGD

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE

Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive Counsel
following an investigation relating to, and admissions made by, the Respondents. It
does not make findings against any persons or entities other than the Respondents
and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document as constituting or
evidencing findings against any other persons or entities since they are not parties to
the proceedings.
1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for Statutory
Audit in the UK and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the “AEP”), revised in
June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the investigation, prosecution
and sanctioning of breaches of Relevant Requirements.
1.2. The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined terms
are also used within this document. Where terms defined in the AEP are used, they
appear in italics.
1.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:
1.3.1.
“FY2019” means the financial year ended 31 December 2019, “FY2019
financial statements” means the financial statements of Stirling Water

Page 2 of 26

Seafield Finance plc (“SWSF”) for that period, and “FY2019 Audit” means the
Statutory Audit of the FY2019 financial statements.
1.3.2.
“FY2009” means the financial year ended 31 March 2009, “FY2009 financial
statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and “FY2009
Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2009 financial statements.
1.3.3.
“FY2018” means the financial year ended 31 December 2018, “FY2018
financial statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and
“FY2018 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2018 financial statements.
1.3.4.
“FY2020” means the financial year ended 31 December 2020, “FY2020
financial statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and
“FY2020 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2020 financial statements.
1.3.5.
“Respondents” means:
1.3.5.1. Ernst & Young LLP (“EY”) which was the Statutory Audit Firm for the
FY2019 Audit and all prior audits since the FY2009 Audit.
1.3.5.2. Mr Christopher Jules Voogd, who was the Statutory Auditor of SWSF
for the FY2019 Audit and signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf of
EY.
1.4. In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents. A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued
by Executive Counsel on 18 November 2024 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation
to the conduct of the Respondents in respect of the FY2019 Audit only. The
Respondents provided written agreement to the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice,
pursuant to Rule 105 of the AEP, on 25 November 2024.
1.5. The Convener subsequently appointed an Independent Reviewer, pursuant to Rule 106
of the AEP, to consider the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice. On 11 December
2024, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this Final Settlement
Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.
1.6. In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP, this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out:
1.6.1.
the breaches of Relevant Requirement(s), with reasons;
1.6.2.
the Sanctions imposed on the Respondents, with reasons; and
1.6.3.
the amount payable by the Respondents in respect of Executive Counsel’s
Costs.
1.7. This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:

Page 3 of 26

1.7.1.
Section 2: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.7.2.
Section 3: Background;
1.7.3.
Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
1.7.4.
Section 5: Details of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.7.5.
Section 6: Sanctions; and
1.7.6.
Section 7: Costs.
2.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
2.1. SWSF is part of an international group of companies (the “Group”), the parent company
of which is headquartered in Europe. SWSF raises funds for other Group companies
and since 2002 it has had bonds admitted to trading on the Main Market of the London
Stock Exchange (“LSE”). As a result, since 2002 SWSF has been and remains a Public
Interest Entity (“PIE”) for the purposes of audit regulation.
2.2. Since 17 June 2016 the Companies Act 20061 has, in summary, imposed a “maximum
engagement period” of ten consecutive years for a Statutory Audit Firm so acting in
respect of a PIE, unless the Statutory Audit Firm was subsequently re-appointed during
that period following a public tender process. These provisions impose requirements,
commonly referred to as Mandatory Firm Rotation (“MFR”) requirements, which have
effect for financial years of companies beginning on or after 17 June 2016. The FRC’s
Revised Ethical Standard (“the Ethical Standard”) imposed a separate obligation to
comply with those requirements. By carrying out the FY2019 Audit, EY breached those
statutory provisions and the Ethical Standard, and both Respondents breached ISA (UK)
200 (Revised June 2016) (“ISA 200”) and ISA (UK) 220 (Revised June 2016) (Updated
July 2017) (“ISA 220”), in relation to the MFR requirements. It is not alleged that the
FY2019 Audit otherwise failed to meet Relevant Requirements or that the FY2019
financial statements were misstated.
2.3. The Companies Act 2006, as amended by the Statutory Auditors and Third Country
Auditors Regulations 2016 and 2017, gave effect to Article 17(1) of the EU Audit
Regulation2, which provided:
“Duration of the audit engagement

1 Sections 489C and 494ZA of the Companies Act 2006.
2 Regulation (EU) No. 537/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council dated 16 April 2014 (“the EU
Audit Regulation”)

Page 4 of 26

A public-interest entity shall appoint a statutory auditor or an audit firm for an initial
engagement of at least one year. The engagement may be renewed. Neither the initial
engagement of a particular statutory auditor or audit firm, nor this in combination with
any renewed engagements therewith shall exceed a maximum duration of 10 years.”
2.4. The purpose of the MFR requirement is to ensure the Statutory Audit Firm’s
independence, and the perception of independence, by either rotating off a PIE audit
engagement after ten years or taking part in a public tender to retain the audit. Recital
(21) to the EU Audit Regulation puts it as follows:
“In order to address the familiarity threat and therefore reinforce the independence of
statutory auditors and audit firms, it is important to establish a maximum duration of the
audit engagement of a statutory auditor or an audit firm in a particular audited entity. In
addition, as a means of strengthening the independence of the statutory auditor or the
audit firm, reinforcing professional scepticism, and increasing audit quality, this
Regulation provides for the following alternatives for an extension of the maximum
duration: regular and open mandatory retendering or the appointment of more than one
statutory auditor or audit firm by public-interest entities.”
2.5. In June 2016 the FRC published the Ethical Standard which included compliance with
the MFR requirements. Paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical Standard provided:
“Public Interest Entities and Other Listed Entities
Audit Firm Rotation
The requirements for audit firm rotation, implementing the relevant provisions of Article
17 of the EU Audit Regulation, are set out in legislation.3 The firm shall ensure that it
does not accept or continue an audit engagement that would cause those requirements
to not be complied with.”
2.6. MFR is a clear and well-known mandatory requirement enshrined in primary legislation
since 17 June 2016 through amendment to the Companies Act 2006. Furthermore, MFR
is an integral part of the ethical requirements to ensure auditor independence, and the
perception of independence, and is a key area of responsibility for a Statutory Auditor
which cannot be delegated.
2.7. As is set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice:

3 The Ethical Standard refers to sections 487 and 489 of the Companies Act 2006; the updated applicable
references are sections 489C and 494ZA.

Page 5 of 26

2.7.1.
EY was appointed auditor of SWSF for the FY2009 Audit without a public tender
process. It remained the Statutory Audit Firm of SWSF for all financial years up
to and including FY2019 without a public tender in any subsequent period.
2.7.2.
During the planning of the FY2020 Audit in early February 2021, EY identified
a potential breach of the MFR requirements, when the senior manager was
completing the continuance procedures for the FY2020 Audit. By the end of
April 2021 the Respondents concluded that they were in breach of the statutory
requirements for MFR, set out at paragraph 2.2 above, which meant that EY
should not have continued with the audit engagement of SWSF beyond
completion of the FY2018 Audit without having been re-appointed following a
public tender.
2.7.3.
EY resigned the engagement for the FY2020 Audit on 29 April 2021. It therefore
did not conduct the FY2020 Audit. EY informed the FRC of its resignation as
SWSF’s Statutory Audit Firm due to a breach of MFR requirements, on 30 April
2021, as it was required to do in accordance with the Companies Act 2006.
2.7.4.
When the Respondents subsequently reported further details of the ethical
breach to the FRC, on 4 November 2021, as part of EY’s bi-annual reporting
covering the period 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2021, they acknowledged
that by carrying out the FY2019 Audit, EY breached the maximum ten year
engagement period set out in the Companies Act 2006 and the Ethical
Standard. On 5 October 2022, before the FRC’s investigation into this matter
commenced, the Respondents provided the FRC’s Case Examiner with a copy
of an internal memorandum that EY had produced in May 2021 which detailed
the circumstances leading to the breach and identified the factors which in EY’s
view contributed to the breach.
2.7.5.
The FRC and EY have separately identified the following factors that
contributed to the breach occurring.
2.7.5.1. The lack of any centralised monitoring of MFR by EY.
2.7.5.2. EY’s internal electronic form that was used for acceptance and
continuance of each client engagement, was known as the Process
for Acceptance of Clients and Engagements (the “PACE” form). The
PACE form used for the FY2019 Audit (hereafter the “FY2019 PACE”)
contained multiple choice questions, one of which (question 2.2.1)
allowed the FY2019 Audit team to select (in error) an option which
stated that the MFR requirements did not apply to SWSF in FY2019,

Page 6 of 26

despite the FY2019 PACE showing that SWSF was a PIE and thus
automatically subject to MFR.
2.7.5.3. The failure by the FY2019 Audit team, including Mr Voogd, to notice
the error outlined at paragraph 2.7.5.2 above when approving the draft
PACE FY2019, despite question 2.2.1 specifically asking whether the
lead engagement partner, in this case Mr Voogd, had confirmed that
the firm was eligible for reappointment.
2.7.5.4. EY’s systems and processes allowed the FY2019 Audit team to
access, complete and upload an out-of-date version of the relevant
workpaper template when performing a separate independence
assessment (the “independence workpaper”), during the FY2019
Audit,
to
assess
EY’s
compliance
with
the
independence
requirements. That template did not contain questions regarding the
correct MFR requirements in force at the time of the FY2019 Audit.
2.7.5.5. The auditor’s report in the FY2019 financial statements, signed by Mr
Voogd, (and the auditor’s report in the FY2018 financial statements
signed by Mr Voogd’s predecessor4) disclosed a duration of EY’s audit
engagement that exceeded ten years. Neither Mr Voogd nor any other
member of the FY2019 Audit team challenged the compatibility of this
disclosure with the MFR requirements. Mr Voogd assumed
(incorrectly) that the issue of MFR had arisen and been resolved in
earlier years during which there had been a tender process at Group
level.
2.7.6.
Having identified and then reported this issue in 2021, EY has taken a number
of steps to prevent recurrence of a breach of the MFR requirements.
2.8. Section 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the detailed breaches of
Relevant Requirements.
2.9. This Final Settlement Decision Notice imposes the following Sanctions in respect of the
Respondents:

4 The audit report for the FY2018 financial statements identified that the period of total uninterrupted engagement
was 11 years, however, given the referenced change in accounting period, the total was in fact 10 years and 9
months. The breach occurred in relation to the FY2019 Audit, as opposed to the FY2018 Audit, as at 1 January
2018 (i.e. the first day of the financial year for the 2018 Audit) the engagement had not yet reached a duration of
10 years which runs from the start of the financial year for which the auditor was first appointed (which in this
case was 1 April 2008), as set out in section 494ZA of the Companies Act 2006.

Page 7 of 26

EY
2.9.1. a financial sanction of £500,000, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating
factors, and subject to a discount of 35% for admissions and early settlement so
that the financial sanction payable is £325,000;
2.9.2. a published statement in the form of a severe reprimand;
2.9.3. a declaration that the FY2019 Audit report signed on behalf of EY did not satisfy
the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice;
and
2.9.4. an order, in the terms set down at Section 6 below, designed to prevent the
recurrence of the contravention
Mr Voogd
2.9.5. a financial sanction of £50,000, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating factors,
and subject to a discount of 35% for admissions and early settlement so that the
financial sanction payable is £32,500;
2.9.6. a published statement in the form of a severe reprimand; and
2.9.7. a declaration that the FY2019 Audit report signed by Mr Voogd did not satisfy
the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice.
3.
BACKGROUND
3.1. In 2023, EY had audit fee income of £737 million, 132 audit principals and 216 PIE audit
clients.5 In 2019, EY had 252 PIE audit clients.6
3.2. Mr Voogd is a partner of EY. He was admitted as a member of the Institute of Chartered
Accountants of England and Wales in 1990 and has been a partner of EY since 1999.
Mr Voogd is an experienced Assurance Partner. He signed the FY2019 Audit report, on
behalf of EY, in respect of the FY2019 financial statements of SWSF on 23 April 2020.
FY2019 was Mr Voogd’s first year as Statutory Auditor for SWSF.
3.3. SWSF is a wholly owned subsidiary of a UK parent company, which is itself a wholly
owned subsidiary of a European parent company that at all material times was an audit
client of EY’s European audit entity. The FY2019 financial statements included the
following description of SWSF in the Directors’ Strategic Report:

5 Figure 33, pages 47-8, Key Facts and Trends in the Accountancy Profession 2024.
6 Figure 33, page 43, Key Facts and Trends in the Accountancy Profession 2020.

Page 8 of 26

“The principal activity of Stirling Water Seafield Finance plc (“the Company”) is to raise
funds to enable other UK&I group companies to upgrade and operate waste water
treatment facilities and provide services relating to the treatment and disposal of sewage
sludge in relation to the Almond Valley, Seafield and Esk (“AVSE”) catchment areas.
The Company is registered and domiciled in the United Kingdom.
The Company is part of the [international parent company group] (“the Group”) which is
defined as all companies under the control of the ultimate parent company, …,
headquartered in [a European city]. The Company is also a member of the “UK&I group”,
a division of the Group, based in the UK and Ireland and involved in the provision of
waste, water and energy services and directly or indirectly under the ownership of [a
UK parent company].”
3.4. SWSF is and was at all material times a financing company with no direct employees. It
raised funds for other Group companies by the issue of bonds which were admitted to
trading on the Main Market of the LSE. These bonds were issued on 4 July 2002 and
are due for repayment on 26 September 2026. The FY2019 financial statements
reported the amount owing on these bonds as at 31 December 2019 as £46.2 million;
income from ordinary activities after taxation for FY2019 was £nil and the statement of
financial position shows equity shareholders’ funds amounting to £50,000.
3.5. By reason of having its bonds admitted to trading on the Main Market of the LSE, SWSF
has been a PIE since admission in 2002 and was a PIE at the time of the FY2019 Audit.
The Statutory Auditors and Third Country Auditors Regulations 2016 (“SATCAR 2016”)
defines a PIE in Regulation 2 as including “an issuer whose transferable securities are
admitted to trading on a regulated market”. Materially the same definition of PIE was
provided by Article 2(13) of Directive 2006/43/EC on Statutory Audits and is set out in
the Companies Act 2006.
3.6. FY2019 was Mr Voogd’s first year as Statutory Auditor for SWSF, although he had
previously been engaged on the Statutory Audits of other UK entities within the Group
(acting as Statutory Auditor for two other related Group entities in 2017 and 2018, and
a further one in in 2018). In 2019, he became Statutory Auditor for approximately 14
further entities within the wider Group, including SWSF and its immediate parent
company.
3.7. The combined audit fees for SWSF's immediate parent company and its two subsidiaries
(including SWSF) were £21,000 for FY2019.

Page 9 of 26

3.8. When Mr Voogd took over the FY2019 Audit, a new senior manager and manager, were
appointed to the FY2019 Audit team. Other members of the audit team remained
consistent from FY2018 to FY2019, as well as the Engagement Quality Review Partner.
4.
RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
4.1. Rule 1 of the AEP states that Relevant Requirements has the meaning set out in
Regulation 5(11) of SATCAR 2016.
4.2. The Relevant Requirements relevant to Executive Counsel’s Final Settlement Decision
Notice are those effective for audits of financial statements for financial periods ending
on 31 December 2019.
4.3. The Relevant Requirements referred to in this Final Settlement Decision Notice are the
following:
4.3.1.
Sections 489C and 494ZA of the Companies Act 20067 (Part 16);
4.3.2.
Article 17 of the EU Audit Regulation;
4.3.3.
ISA 200 (Overall objectives of the independent auditor and the conduct of an
audit in accordance with international standards on auditing);
4.3.4.
ISA 220 (Quality Control for an Audit of Financial Statements);
4.3.5.
the International Standard on Quality Control (UK) 1 (Revised June 2016)
(“ISQC 1”) (Quality Control for Firms that perform Audits and Reviews of
Financial
Statements,
and
other
Assurance
and
Related
Services
Engagements); and
4.3.6.
the Ethical Standard.
4.4. Extracts from the above, setting out those parts which are of particular relevance to the
breaches of Relevant Requirements in this case, are set out in Appendix 1 hereto.
4.5. As the Statutory Auditor responsible for the FY2019 Audit, Mr Voogd was responsible
for the overall quality of the FY2019 Audit and the direction, supervision, and
performance of the FY2019 Audit in compliance with the professional standards and
applicable legal and regulatory requirements (ISA 220, paragraph 15(a)).

7 The Ethical Standard refers to sections 487 and 489 of the Companies Act 2006; the updated applicable
references are sections 489C and 494ZA.

Page 10 of 26

4.6. In addition to breaches of Relevant Requirements directly applicable to the firm, as the
Statutory Audit Firm responsible for the FY2019 Audit, EY is responsible for any
established breaches of Relevant Requirements on the part of its partners or employees.
5.
BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
Breach 1 – Breach by EY of applicable statutory MFR requirements
EY breached section 489C of the Companies Act 2006, and thereby paragraph 3.9
of the Ethical Standard, by undertaking the FY2019 Audit.
5.1. As noted above, EY was required to comply with the Companies Act 2006 and the
Ethical Standard as regards MFR. The Companies Act 2006, (which gives effect to the
EU Audit Regulation), specifies a ten year maximum period for audit engagements of a
PIE, subject to exceptions explained in the following paragraph.8
5.2. Neither the Ethical Standard nor the statutory provisions set out above provide for
exceptions to the ten year period, save where a public tender is carried out during the
ten year period or, in exceptional circumstances, the maximum engagement period is
extended with the approval of the FRC. There can be no safeguards put in place to
mitigate the threats caused to independence by exceeding the “maximum engagement
period”.
5.3. The “maximum engagement period” is defined in section 494ZA of the Companies Act
2006. Applying that definition to EY’s audit of SWSF results in a maximum engagement
period that ends with “the last financial year of the company to begin within the period
of 10 years beginning with the first day of the first financial year of the maximum
engagement period”. On the facts of this case, the first day of the first financial year of
the maximum engagement period was 1 April 2008. The last financial year of the
company to begin within a period of ten years from 1 April 2008 was FY2018.
Accordingly, the maximum engagement period permitted, absent a public tender or
exceptional circumstances, ended with the completion of the FY2018 Audit.
5.4. EY breached section 489C of the Companies Act 2006 and paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical
Standard, by accepting its appointment as Statutory Auditor for FY2019 Audit.

8 Sections 489C and 494ZA of the Companies Act 2006; paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical Standard; Article 17 of the
EU Audit Regulation.

Page 11 of 26

Breach 2 – Breaches by EY and Mr Voogd in relation to MFR requirements
The Respondents failed to comply with paragraphs 11, 12 and 15 of ISA 220 and as
a consequence failed to meet the requirement in paragraph 14 of ISA 200, in that Mr
Voogd failed to:
(a)
form an appropriate conclusion on EY’s compliance with independence
requirements that applied to the FY2019 audit engagement;
(b)
satisfy himself that appropriate procedures regarding the continuance of
the FY2019 audit engagement had been followed and to determine that
the conclusions reached in that regard were appropriate and consistent
with the MFR requirements; and
(c)
ensure that the auditor’s report in the FY2019 Audit was appropriate in
the circumstances.
5.5. Under ISA 200 and ISA 220, Mr Voogd was under specific obligations as the Statutory
Auditor in relation to the FY2019 Audit. These requirements were the individual
responsibility of Mr Voogd as Statutory Auditor.
5.6. Paragraph 14 of ISA 200 required Mr Voogd to comply with relevant ethical
requirements, including those pertaining to independence such as the MFR requirement
in paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical Standard, in relation to financial statement audit
engagements.
5.7. Under ISA 220 Mr Voogd was required to form a conclusion on compliance with
independence requirements that applied to the audit engagement (ISA 220, paragraph
11). He was also obliged under ISA 220 (paragraph 12) to be satisfied that appropriate
procedures regarding the continuance of the FY2019 Audit had been followed and to
determine that the conclusions reached in that regard were appropriate.
5.8. The Explanatory Material in ISA 220, at paragraph A8, provides guidance in relation to
the engagement partner’s obligation under ISA 220 paragraph 12. Paragraph A8
identifies ISQC 1 as a source of requirements on Statutory Audit Firms regarding
obtaining information necessary before deciding whether to continue an existing
engagement. paragraph A8 then identifies categories of information that will assist the
engagement partner in this area, including “whether the firm ... can comply with relevant
ethical requirements”.
5.9. Paragraph 15(b) of ISA 220 requires the engagement partner to take responsibility for
the auditor’s report being appropriate in the circumstances.

Page 12 of 26

5.10. Mr Voogd failed to comply with his obligations under ISA 200, paragraph 14, and ISA
220, paragraphs 11, and 12 by accepting EY’s appointment as Statutory Auditor for the
FY2019 Audit in breach of MFR requirements. Mr Voogd failed to comply with ISA 220,
paragraph 15 by approving an auditor’s report which incorrectly represented that EY
was independent of SWSF in accordance with relevant ethical requirements.
Particulars of Breaches
5.11. As at 19 November 2019, at the point Mr Voogd took over the FY2019 Audit, no audit
work had been performed. He met with the outgoing Statutory Auditor face to face in
Glasgow for the handover or “kick-off” meeting. In interview, Mr Voogd stated that during
the meeting it was made clear to him that SWSF was a PIE but he did not recall any
discussion of the MFR requirements.
5.12. On 6 December 2019, Mr Voogd approved the FY2019 PACE form. This form had been
prepared by members of the FY2019 Audit team, who answered a question on it by
stating that MFR requirements did not apply to SWSF. This answer was incorrect, as
MFR requirements had applied to all audits of PIEs since June 2016. The effect of
selecting “N/A” was that no further MFR questions were triggered. The question
specifically addresses the lead engagement partner’s responsibility in this area and read
as follows:
Question 2.2.1: Has the lead engagement partner for the audit engagement confirmed
that the firm is eligible for reappointment as auditor and is therefore compliance [sic]
with the mandatory firm rotation requirements for Public Interest Entities as prescribed
by law of the applicable EU/EEA Member State?
o Yes
o No
o N/A – Mandatory firm rotation rules do not apply to the audit of this entity.
This question and the selected answer, “N/A”, was apparent on the face of the FY2019
PACE form itself. Mr Voogd accepts that he approved the FY2019 PACE form without
noticing this error.
5.13. On 23 April 2020, Mr Voogd also approved the independence workpaper that the
FY2019 Audit team completed in relation to the FY2019 Audit. The preparer had used
an out-of-date version of the workpaper, which did not contain questions regarding the
correct MFR requirements in force at the time of the FY2019 Audit but rather referred to
previous requirements. These questions only raised the issue of firm rotation for FTSE

Page 13 of 26

350 clients, not all PIEs. Mr Voogd did not notice that the preparer had in error used an
out-of-date workpaper.
5.14. On 28 April 2020, Mr Voogd signed the audit report contained in the FY2019 financial
statements, approving that report for and on behalf of EY. That audit report included the
following statement three paragraphs above Mr Voogd’s signature on behalf of EY and
on the same page: “The period of total uninterrupted engagement including previous
renewals and reappointments is 12 years, covering the years ended 31 March 2009 to
31 December 2019 (the financial period changed in 2012 with the addition of a 9 month
period to 31 December 2012).”9 Mr Voogd explained in interview that because the audit
report contained in the FY2018 financial statements had referred to a period of total
uninterrupted engagement of 11 years, this wording did not suggest to him that there
was an issue with MFR in relation to the FY2019 Audit. Nonetheless, before signing the
audit report in the FY2019 financial statements Mr Voogd should have satisfied himself
that his assumption was correct and that EY had complied with the MFR requirements
in undertaking the FY2019 Audit.
5.15. The “Basis for opinion” within the auditor’s report in the FY2019 financial statements
states: “We are independent of the Company in accordance with the ethical
requirements that are relevant to our audit of the financial statements in the UK,
including the FRC’s Ethical Standard as applied to listed public interest entities, and we
have fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements.”
This statement was incorrect, and therefore Mr Voogd failed to ensure that the auditor’s
report was appropriate.
5.16. In these circumstances the Respondents’ conduct breached paragraph 14 of ISA 200
and paragraphs 11, 12 and 15 of ISA 220:
5.16.1. Mr Voogd failed to form an appropriate conclusion on compliance with the MFR
requirements that applied to the audit engagement.
5.16.2. He did not satisfy himself that appropriate procedures had been followed to
conclude that EY could continue with the audit engagement and conduct the
FY2019 Audit in compliance with MFR requirements.
5.16.3. He failed to conduct an adequate review to identify the error in the auditor’s
report in the FY2019 financial statements. The obvious error in the FY2019
PACE, the use of the incorrect independence workpaper and/or the disclosure

9 Whilst the audit report for the FY2019 financial statements identified that the period of total uninterrupted
engagement was 12 years, given the referenced change in accounting period, the total was in fact 11 years and 9
months.

Page 14 of 26

made in the auditor’s report in the FY2019 financial statements of a 12 year
tenure were “red flags” that should have led to the identification by Mr Voogd of
the breach by EY of MFR requirements in FY2019.
Breach 3 – Breach by EY of quality control obligations regarding ethical
requirements
EY failed to:
(a)
establish policies and procedures designed to provide it with reasonable
assurance that the firm maintains independence where required by
relevant ethical requirements, in particular policies and procedures that
require the accumulation and communication of relevant information to
appropriate personnel so that the firm and its personnel can readily
determine whether they satisfy independence requirements, in breach of
the obligation in paragraph 22(c)(i) of ISQC 1 (as imposed by paragraph
21 of ISQC 1); and
(b)
assess whether the conditions for the duration of the audit engagement
in accordance with the EU Audit Regulation were complied with, before
continuing with the engagement for the FY2019 Audit, in breach of
paragraph 27R-(2)(b) of ISQC 1.
5.17. Paragraph 22(c)(i) of ISQC 1 (as imposed by paragraph 21 of ISQC 1) and the Ethical
Standard imposed an obligation on EY to establish policies and procedures designed to
provide reasonable assurance in relation to the relevant ethical requirements. That
obligation included establishing policies and procedures that “require” the accumulation
and communication of relevant information, so that EY could readily determine whether
it satisfied independence requirements such as the ten year MFR requirement.
5.18. EY was also required to assess, before continuing an audit engagement, whether the
conditions for the duration of the audit engagement in accordance with UK law were
complied with (ISQC 1, paragraph 27R-2(b)).
5.19. EY failed to comply with these obligations in the following ways, which caused or
contributed to its breach of MFR requirements by accepting its appointment to perform
the FY2019 Audit.

Particulars of Breaches

5.20. At the time of the breach of MFR requirements in FY2019, EY’s policies and procedures
to ensure compliance with MFR relied upon engagement teams considering MFR
requirements throughout the audit, using the PACE form and an independence
workpaper. These policies and procedures failed to require the accumulation and
communication of relevant information to appropriate personnel so that EY could readily
determine whether it met the independence requirements. In particular they did not
require the accumulation and communication of information regarding the length of the
audit engagement and thus how many years were left out of the ten years permitted as
a maximum engagement length for the audit of a PIE.
5.21. By FY2019, EY had established at firm level certain policies and procedures in relation
to the accumulation and communication of information relevant to independence
requirements, as described below, but those policies and procedures were not sufficient
to comply with the obligation in ISQC 1, paragraph 22(c)(i) (as imposed by paragraph
21 of ISQC 1).
5.21.1. Although EY’s Statutory Auditors were required to populate a Partner Rotation
Database (“PRD”), this was designed to monitor separate requirements which
apply to the rotation of individuals on the audit team rather than the firm as a
whole. The PRD did allow the auditor appointment date to be recorded in a free
text box, but there was no mechanism to allow reporting or monitoring of entries
in that field.
5.21.2. Each year, EY provided an “Annual Independence Confirmation” to EY Global
to confirm that appropriate procedures were in place to monitor compliance with
the EY Global Independence Policy, including, since 2016, in relation to MFR.
In the circumstances at the time of the breach, and given the failings set out in
this PSDN, such confirmation was inappropriate.
5.21.3. The version of the PACE form that was given to engagement teams such as
that on the FY2019 Audit adopted an incorrect procedure regarding MFR since
it (i) allowed the audit team to answer that MFR requirements did not apply to
the audit of a PIE despite the fact that MFR requirements had applied to all
audits of PIEs since June 2016, and (ii) did not require the accumulation of MFR
information from prior years. This would have shown the length of the audit
engagement to date and thus how many years were left out of the ten years
permitted as a maximum engagement length for the audit of PIEs. In turn that
would have allowed EY to prepare for the end of the engagement, for example
putting in place a tender process for a subsequent engagement.

SANCTIONS
6.1. Paragraph 10 of the FRC’s Sanctions Policy (Audit Enforcement Procedure) (the
“Sanctions Policy”) provides that Sanctions are intended to be effective, proportionate
and dissuasive. The reasons for imposing Sanctions are identified in paragraph 11 of
the Sanctions Policy as the following:
6.1.1. to declare and uphold proper standards of conduct amongst Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms and to maintain and enhance the quality and reliability
of future audits;
6.1.2. to maintain and promote public and market confidence in Statutory Auditors and
Statutory Audit Firms and the quality of their audits and in the regulation of the
accountancy profession;
6.1.3. to protect the public from Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms whose
conduct has fallen short of the Relevant Requirements; and
6.1.4. to deter Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms from breaching the
Relevant Requirements relating to Statutory Audit.
6.2. Paragraph 12 of the Sanctions Policy provides that the primary purpose of imposing
Sanctions for breaches of the Relevant Requirements is not to punish, but to protect the
public and the wider public interest.
6.3. In deciding on Sanctions, Executive Counsel has, in summary, considered the following
matters in accordance with the Sanctions Policy.
Nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches
6.4. The Relevant Requirements breached including the Companies Act 2006, the ISAs,
ISQC 1 and the Ethical Standard, are fundamental to ensuring auditor independence,
and ensuring the integrity, objectivity and independence of Statutory Audit.
6.5. Compliance with the Ethical Standard is inherently important as it establishes a
framework of ethical outcomes that are required to be met by the auditor, to provide a

basis for user trust and confidence in the independence, integrity and objectivity of the
practitioner in performing the engagement.10
6.6. Whilst the breaches in relation to the FY2019 Audit relate to only one audit year, the
breaches are serious in that they include a clear breach of the Companies Act 2006 and
the Ethical Standard on the FY2019 Audit and serious individual identifiable failings on
the part of Mr Voogd and the FY2019 Audit team.
6.7. In addition to the breaches in relation to the ethical requirements on the FY2019 Audit,
there were significant firm wide failings within EY, including its compliance with ISQC 1,
which had the potential to impact on other PIE audits over a number of years. Such
breaches relate to the effectiveness of EY’s relevant procedures, systems and internal
control and indicate that the internal review and quality procedures regarding MFR that
were applied at EY in 2019 and 2020 were ineffective.
6.8. It is not alleged that the breaches of Relevant Requirements caused or risked the loss
of significant sums of money for investors or creditors. Nor is it alleged that the FY2019
financial statements were misstated. However, in light of:
6.8.1. the fundamental and well-known mandatory nature of the MFR requirements, the
importance of the Ethical Standard and independence requirements, and the
failure to conduct the FY2019 Audit in accordance with these Relevant
Requirements;
6.8.2. the fact that, as a result of the breaches of Relevant Requirements, EY was
ineligible to conduct the FY2019 Audit and should have resigned; and
6.8.3. the issues identified with EY’s policies, procedures and quality control monitoring
systems;
the breaches in aggregate undermine confidence in the standards of conduct in general
of Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms, and/or in Statutory Audit, and could harm
investor, market and public confidence in the truth and fairness of the financial
statements published by Statutory Auditors or Statutory Audit Firms.
6.9. It is not alleged that the breaches were intentional, nor that the Respondents acted
dishonestly, intentionally or recklessly.
6.10. EY informed the FRC of the breach, in the context of EY’s resignation as Statutory
Auditor and as part of EY’s biannual reporting cycle, in accordance with their statutory
obligations and the Ethical Standard respectively.
